atom.sourceQuote: Rebuilt the route planner for 40 depots at Example Freight.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: Drivers were getting their routes at 6am and the planner ignored road closures, so a lot of deliveries ran late and customers called the depots all morning.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I owned the route planner service, and my manager asked me to fix it before peak season started in November.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: First I sat with the dispatch lead for two mornings to see how they rerouted by hand. Then I added a road closures feed to the planner and re-ran routes at 5am instead of 6am. I shipped it to two depots first and then to the rest.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: Late deliveries went from 12% to 3% in the first month, and the dispatch team stopped rerouting by hand.

atom.what: Moved invoice reminders to a queue
atom.sourceQuote: Moved invoice reminders from a cron job to a queue at Example Billing.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: Invoice reminders went out from a cron job that sometimes ran twice, so customers got duplicate reminders and support had to apologise.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I was asked to make sure every customer got exactly one reminder.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: I moved the reminders onto a queue and gave each reminder a key so the same one could never be sent twice. I wrote a test that ran the job twice on purpose.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: Support stopped getting complaints about duplicate reminders. I don't have exact numbers.

atom.sourceQuote: Helped migrate the user database to Postgres at Example Social.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: So basically, um, the old database was a MySQL box that nobody really wanted to touch, and it was, you know, kind of the thing everyone was scared of, because if it went down the whole app went down, and it had gone down twice that year already.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I was one of three people on the migration. My part was the data copy and checking it.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: We set up the new Postgres database next to the old one. I wrote the copy job and a checker that compared row counts and checksums for every table every night. We ran both databases side by side for three weeks before we switched, and honestly the checker caught a couple of encoding bugs that would have been really bad.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: We switched over on a Sunday night with no downtime, and the checker found zero differences in the last week.

answers.question: Anything else worth telling? (optional, press Enter to skip)
answers.answer: I learned a lot about character encodings.

atom.sourceQuote: Rolled out a caching layer for the product catalogue at Example Shop.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: The product pages were slow during sales, and we wanted a cache in front of the catalogue service.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I designed and rolled out the cache.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: I rolled it out to all traffic at once on a Friday. Prices changed during a sale and the cache kept serving old prices for about an hour before I turned it off. Afterwards I added a way to clear the cache when a price changes and rolled it out again one region at a time.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: The second rollout worked and the pages got faster. The bigger change was me: I don't ship big changes to all traffic at once anymore.

atom.what: Pushed back on a launch date
atom.sourceQuote: Delayed a payments launch by one week to finish fraud checks at Example Pay.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: Product wanted to launch card payments on a fixed date for a marketing campaign, but the fraud checks weren't finished.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I was the engineer responsible for the payment flow, so I had to decide whether it was safe to launch.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: I wrote down what could go wrong without the fraud checks and went through it with the product manager. She disagreed at first because of the campaign. We agreed to launch one week later, and I stayed in the campaign meetings so marketing could move their dates.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: We launched one week late with the fraud checks in place, and marketing moved the campaign by the same week.

atom.sourceQuote: Built the first reporting dashboard for 3 regional managers at Example Retail.

answers.question: Situation: what was going on, and why did it matter?
answers.answer: The regional managers said they wanted better reporting, but nobody could say what that meant.

answers.question: Task: what were you responsible for?
answers.answer: I was asked to build something useful for them with no spec.

answers.question: Action: what did you do, step by step?
answers.answer: I asked each of the 3 managers to show me the spreadsheet they used every Monday. I found they all tracked the same four numbers, so I built a dashboard with just those four and showed it to them every week, changing it based on what they said.

answers.question: Result: what changed? Any numbers you can stand behind?
answers.answer: After a month they stopped sending their Monday spreadsheets around and used the dashboard instead.
